speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head O of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I declare that I am a doctor working at a public hospital.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will speak on our healthcare system and thinking outside the box.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, we have already started thinking outside the box in healthcare policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there are other boxes we need to think outside of, as part of the next bound of healthcare policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, we also need to think outside the box of space and place – bringing the care, bringing the subsidy to where the patient is, where the person in need is.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some public hospitals have been testing hospital-at-home services, or what is called mobile inpatient care at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Ministry of Health (MOH) provide an update on the progress of these efforts?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can we make it easier as well for MediShield Life and MediSave to be claimable for care that is delivered to patients at home where medically necessary?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to speak also about the ecosystem of care because bringing care closer to home goes beyond medical care, nursing care or allied healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It must also look at Government programmes that support the sick and unwell.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I remember my Clementi resident who passed away.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We got to know each other over my eight, coming to nine years in Clementi.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We visited her in hospital, visited her funeral wake.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She was getting more ill, getting more frail – more frail, more prone to falls.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She was ill with kidney failure for many years, on peritoneal dialysis, finding it heavy going doing her own peritoneal dialysis at home every night.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She applied for a migrant domestic worker levy concession – maid levy concession.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But she was not old enough to fit the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) aged person scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, she applied to the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) under MOH.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She was told that because she did not always require assistance with at least one of the activities of daily living (ADL), did not always require assistance with one ADL and so, she could not qualify.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But I ask the Ministry, could the ADL have been looked at in context?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Could the ADL have been considered in context of someone who was frail, getting more and more frail, many medical conditions and on peritoneal dialysis at home?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Could it have been asked by the agencies, would the patient – would the resident – find it difficult to do peritoneal dialysis at home without the extra help?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if you speak with real-world practitioners on the ground, there are residents – there are patients – who may not fit the technical criteria, always requires assistance with at least one ADL.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many who met my resident in person would have found her frail, even if she did not fit the letter of the policy, many would have felt she fit the spirit of the policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I call upon MOH to consider such situations, see if there is a way to take into account the medical situation of the patient – the spirit of the policy, in addition to the letter.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is another group of patients – palliative care patients with a limited lifespan, life-limiting disease, not much time left.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And likewise, I call upon MOH, can our agencies, in assessing the concessionary levy for migrant domestic workers in the approval process for frail patients on home peritoneal dialysis, who already find it difficult to cope without a helper, can they be considered more holistically?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For patients with a serious life-limiting disease, not much time left, can they be considered holistically as well?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Back in January 2022, two years ago, I asked a question in Parliament, how many specialist outpatient clinic visits a patient might have in an individual year at a public hospital?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Imagine being a patient or a caregiver, this many visits, trying to hold down a job, because we know that not every employer allows flexible working arrangements.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know that not every job makes that flexibility possible.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know that while some employers are kind, there are employers who can be one kind.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, Mr Chairman, this is something our agencies need to look at.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I called upon MOH to look into this two years ago during the MOH Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MOH give an update on how they are looking at this?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some might ask, why should MOH subsidise home medical care, care closer to home, in order to save jobs for patients and caregivers?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we already accept in principle, in other Ministries, that subsidy and funding can be used to save jobs or create a more level playing field for workers who encounter disadvantages.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, MOM has the Enabling Employment Credit to help persons with disabilities find work in an uneven job market.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: MOM has the Uplifting Employment Credit to help people find a second chance in life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: MOM has the Part-Time Re-Employment Grant to help senior workers who need part-time employment opportunities or flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, given this precedent in other Ministries across the whole of Government, I call upon MOH and the Government as a whole to look at access to home medical care and home medical treatment through the lens of a coordinated approach to economic and social policies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, if better home care helps save the job of a patient, if it helps save the job and career of a caregiver, can the case be made at whole of Government with MOH, MOM and MOF looking together at this?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In particular, can we further reduce the visits to a public hospital for patients who are undergoing means testing for assistance and MediFund?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2016, nearly eight years ago, I asked in Parliament: can we make it smoother for patients on MediFund who are seeking treatment across different public hospitals in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can we also empower the Social Service Offices (SSOs) or the local Family Service Centres (FSCs) or the Active Ageing Centres (AACs) to assist the public hospitals, medical social workers, to do some of these means test assessments?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This can reduce the need for an additional trip to see the medical social worker at the hospital.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Reduce the need for additional appointments, especially for lower-wage, lower-resource families for whom travel may be more challenging.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On patients with mobility needs, can we also make it easier to find access to subsidised transport for patients who are less mobile with medically necessary visits to the clinic or medically necessary trips to receive treatment?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some months back, a fellow Singaporean and her family – this fellow Singaporean was undergoing treatment for a serious illness at a public hospital – shared about how the multiple visits to clinics for treatment to and fro, this, over the span of a month, especially where some trips were made during rush or peak hour.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will now speak on home personal care because care for a senior goes beyond the clinic and we must look at their daily life at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many seniors want to stay in the community where friends, coffee shop "kawans", "kakis" are.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But some need help with daily living, showering, cleaning up the home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Support for home personal care can make the difference in whether someone is in the community or later institutionalised.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MOH look at how we can support seniors better on home personal care?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On seniors living alone, falls are a worry for our seniors, not just the injury but some seniors having fallen, cannot get up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If the senior is socially isolated, living alone, it may mean not getting help till someone passes by.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or worse still, what happens if the senior has fallen, cannot call for help, does not have anyone coming by and the community only discovers later after that senior has died?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Two years ago, in a Parliamentary Question in 2022, I asked MOH about using technology to help look out for frail seniors who had fallen at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to speak about the upcoming new Clementi Polyclinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today's Clementi Polyclinic is in the town centre, near to the Clementi MRT station, near to Clementi Bus Interchange, with sheltered, barrier-free access for many blocks around the Clementi Town Centre.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There would be addition of new features – bigger polyclinic, more capacity, more services.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there also would be one important subtraction.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many residents no longer will have sheltered last-mile barrier-free access to the new location.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many residents who previously had sheltered last-mile access will have to cross Clementi Avenue 3.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For less mobile seniors with a walking stick or mobility aid, imagine holding an umbrella in the rain.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If you are an elderly caregiver pushing your loved one in a wheelchair, imagine doing that in rainy weather and trying to hold an umbrella for the two of you at the same time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, this crossing is right next to Clementi MRT station.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Especially since we have many Clementi residents who today attend the existing Clementi Polyclinic with sheltered barrier-free access and will find it harder to get to the new polyclinic location on a rainy day, and it would benefit young families as well, children in prams being brought by their parents or sometimes their grandparents too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I call upon MOH and LTA to work together, see what can be done, whether this sheltered last-mile barrier-free access can be costed and factored in fiscally as part of the project holistically, because access to care goes beyond having a new, larger polyclinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is also about whether frail seniors with mobility needs can feasibly get to that polyclinic the same way they did to the existing polyclinic in the Clementi Town Centre.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I said to Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, eight years ago in 2016, during an Adjournment Motion debate when Deputy Prime Minister was Minister for National Development, and I quote, “When we add new innovations, we must be mindful not to subtract from what came before, especially when it affects the vulnerable and disadvantaged among us.” Sir, the current Minister for Transport used to serve at MOH.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The current Health Minister used to look after MOT.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because even as we think outside the box, we also have to ask ourselves are the existing boxes big enough, deep enough.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, do we have enough capacity, enough capability?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is MOH getting ready for what happens when there is more health screening as part of Healthier SG?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Residents with pre-existing illness, did not know they were ill, but having gone for screening, having had illness discovered, will need follow-up, will need treatment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are we looking at the projected increase in demand?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is MOH taking a good look at how much time is needed to deliver holistic care, 21st century care, in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because, whether you persuade someone to stop smoking, help someone with a mental health crisis, or support someone with a life-threatening illness and with limited time, all this needs holistic care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I said 11 years ago in The Straits Times and last year in Parliament, if a clinic is too busy and consultation times are too short, it becomes harder to promote health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When our decision-makers understand the actual amount of work that is needed, the ground situation, it is like flying an airplane.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even the best pilot needs to know what is the altitude, what is the air speed, how much is in the fuel tank.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On healthcare financing, when thinking outside the box, we need to keep the toolbox stocked with new tools.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, in summary, Mr Speaker, we will need resources, energy and imagination for tomorrow to keep our healthcare system fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, having to be hospitalised is physiologically and emotionally stressful in many ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fortunately, our health workers work hard to minimise the inconveniences of the experience as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, to know that you have to wait long hours for a bed in Singapore does not correspond with what many older Singaporeans in particular expect of our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At their moment of need, many of our seniors and even citizens across various age groups did not believe that they would have to wait hours in a chair in an A&E department or be decamped to beds located at a temporary car park where the lights are never turned off at their moment of critical need.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Imagine being ill and uncomfortable and having to wait 16 hours for a bed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This hospital experience is being narrated anecdotally to me by an increasing number of seniors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would also relieve and better spread the patient load at hospitals where doctors and nurses, allied health workers and staff consistently see higher A&E admissions and bed utilisation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand moves are underway to increase the number of hospitals and polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, piling works have just begun last month for the Eastern Integrated Health Campus in my ward of Eunos in Aljunied Group Representation Constituency, the development of which is expected to take some patient load off Changi General Hospital.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These developments should improve the situation, but it has to account for the rising number of seniors and Singaporeans who inevitably will have to tap onto the healthcare system in some shape or form, and also to account for the rising healthcare manpower needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, there have been reports of patients preferring to stay in a hospital longer than they are supposed to, despite being medically fit for discharge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One report cited an expert as postulating, for example, that three out of 10 patients at the National University Hospital (NUH) or their family members have to contend with discharge issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While each situation would have to be looked at on a case-by-case basis, such patients can exacerbate the problems faced by the primary healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How many patients were labelled as overstayers in our public hospitals in 2023, and how serious is this problem?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry share its plans on how it intends to expand home care services over the next five years as well, to reduce patient load in hospitals, and so as to ensure that the load on our healthcare workers is not more than it needs to be?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling, you can take your four cuts together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In such an at-home care setting, family and community involvement seems crucial to maximise the benefits of patients’ recovery.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This may involve training family members in basic care protocols and procedures to create a conducive and supportive home environment for the recovery of the patient.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that such scale-up can provide more options to patients and caregivers, especially for senior patients who may prefer to recover in the comfort of their own home.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, given an ageing population where healthcare needs will increase and prolong, as well as advancements in medical treatment options that can be more costly, there is a concern on rising healthcare costs that may lead to higher out-of-pocket expenditures for Singaporeans in the years ahead.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another concern is the cost drivers in public hospitals that may increase operating expenditures, which can all indirectly increase bill sizes and out-of-pocket expenses for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, what are the primary drivers behind the increase in healthcare costs in Singapore and how can they contribute to hospital bill sizes?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, what cost control mechanisms are currently in place or will be in place in our public hospitals to mitigate cost increases and ensure healthcare remains affordable?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three, how does MOH intend to help public hospitals manage their costs and become more cost-efficient?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Four, is the MediShield Life coverage expected to continue to be adequate to help Singaporeans defray a substantial portion of their bill sizes and keep out-of-pocket expenditures low?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, how can MediShield Life adapt its coverage to reflect these rising costs while ensuring that the premiums remain financially sustainable for Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the Healthier SG initiative marks a pivotal shift in our national healthcare strategy towards preventive care with an emphasis on community-based health management.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The successful implementation of this initiative relies heavily on the active collaboration between MOH, Primary Care Networks (PCN), polyclinics and private general practitioners (GPs).

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more Singaporeans enrol on this initiative, besides focusing on reaching a wide base, I believe that there must be also healthcare indicators that can show that our population health is improving.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How has the personalised health plans been monitored for the enrolled residents?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, does MOH expect that the prevalence rates for the most common chronic diseases faced by Singaporeans, including high cholesterol, high blood pressure and diabetes to ease or reverse as Healthier SG initiative rolls out?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of our GP clinics are well located in most neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, their involvement in Healthier SG is an important collaboration in the population preventive health approach that we are increasingly taking.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we integrate social prescription and increase access of mental health treatment through our primary care providers in the Healthier SG and other national health strategies, our GPs will increasingly need help in expanding their capacities and capabilities, including receiving comprehensive and continuing training.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially so when areas such as social prescriptions and mental health treatment may be relatively newer areas that our GPs need to increase proficiency in.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask MOH to provide updates on whether it has overall capacity building and professional development plans for our GPs, especially on: one, how are the GPs going to be supported to make time for continuing education training when time away from their clinics can mean opportunity costs from seeing patients in their clinics?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, what are the support and resources provided to GPs on the latest research findings and protocols for the most effective treatment options in common chronic diseases, especially those where we are seeing increasing prevalence rates, such as hypertension?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, for social prescription and mental health treatment, which usually require a multi-disciplinary treatment involvement, how will the GPs be equipped and how will the joint training be done for such multi-disciplinary teams to provide best health intervention to patients who need them?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Second, could the Minister also share whether early indicators suggest that Healthier SG plans are achieving its articulated goals and outcomes?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Is the approach towards better preventive healthcare being realised?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Have both doctors and patients, at the last mile, reported stronger patient-doctor relationships and are patients having better experiences when receiving their care with their primary healthcare provider through Healthier SG?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Third, part of the vision of Healthier SG is that there be more rooted partnerships and the integration of health and social ecosystems of care.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Have partnerships been strongly established with agencies like AIC, the Health Promotion Board (HPB), People's Association (PA) as well as Sport Singapore to realise the vision of Healthier SG?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry share specific examples of how this has been done and expected to evolve over time?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Have there been any barriers in this regard and could the Ministry share the forward steps that can be anticipated in this space?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Are there any changes to be made to the Healthier SG implementation plans, especially towards incorporating the four tiers of the tiered care model and to realise the four articulated focus areas as outlined by the strategy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Healthier SG initiative holds immense promise for transforming our healthcare system towards upstream and preventive care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Understanding the level of public engagement is important to gauge the programme's effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will they include a list of recommended activities tailored to individual needs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I have some concerns regarding its impact on the wider population.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will this expansion lead to patients having to switch GPs to access the full benefits of Healthier SG?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry equip them with the training, tools, and support they need to effectively manage these additional chronic conditions, particularly those requiring specialised knowledge?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to avoid overburdening GPs and jeopardising the quality of care for existing patients.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we witness an increasing number of seniors living alone, the potential for social isolation and unmet care needs becomes a pressing concern.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I want to focus on how we can ensure that our seniors stay active, connected and well-cared for within their communities, aligning with the Age Well SG strategy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could involve metrics on senior well-being, programme effectiveness and cost-efficiency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry implement the shift from insititutionalised care to community and home-based care, highlighting specific initiatives, take-up rates and timelines?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister share the current average waiting time for nursing home beds?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What novel models of care are available to bridge the gap and prevent institutionalisation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, can the Minister update on the progress of rolling out Active Ageing Centres (AACs) to seniors in non-rental flats, ensuring broader accessibility?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will AACs implement initiatives that specifically foster inter-generational relationships, tackling social isolation for seniors while providing learning opportunities for younger generations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we specifically reach out to those seniors who are reluctant to socialise, as they are most vulnerable to loneliness?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourthly, enhancing home-based care for seniors with higher needs is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does the Ministry also have a target of how many patients do we aim to onboard for home-based care?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As home care can be resource-intensive, can the Ministry also share about the long-term financial sustainability of such programmes, especially regarding potential future cost increases and affordability for seniors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we increase public awareness of home-based care?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry raise awareness about this system and other fall detection solutions, especially among seniors who live alone?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the broader level, will the Ministry partner with technology companies to develop similar senior-friendly applications?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These solutions can also be used for social interaction, health monitoring or for accessing services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, building a society where everyone ages well necessitates a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By addressing social isolation, providing accessible care options and investing in community infrastructure and manpower, we can ensure our seniors live fulfilled and dignified lives within their communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my speech on the Motion on supporting healthcare in May last year, I spoke about how hospital bed and medical personnel capacity in our fair nation falls short of what may be expected, not just compared to almost every other advanced economy, but also to our own internal benchmarks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has led to us failing to meet health service quality targets set by MOH.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Things have improved somewhat since then, but capacity still remains constrained.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is a dire need to relieve not only our capacity shortfalls in the short run, but also any projected long-run need.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What this comes down to is a willingness to sacrifice short-run efficiency by accepting a certain amount of redundancy in the interim, at least until the needs inevitably arise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My sense is that this will only occur when our current occupancy rate for hospitals remains substantially below 80%, at least for a certain duration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To achieve this, I believe that the current system can stand to expand its transition care offerings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While still uncommon, there are already several urgent care centres (UCCs) in Singapore, including the reclassification of Alexandra Hospital's A&E department into a UCC, along with several private providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans should be educated about using this channel for non-life-threatening medical emergencies, especially with regard to the substantially shorter wait times compared to A&E.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It can also relieve the pressure on polyclinics to triage such cases for which they are not designed for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government can directly encourage this by providing rebates to insurance companies for encouraging select cases to pursue this route.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Otherwise, if the approach is simply one of delivering more subsidies that exchange for greater health price regulation, economy plus healthcare, the true advantage of the non-profit model may be lost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, I encourage MOH to also look at public health bills.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This situation is alarming and warrants immediate attention.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Regrettably, the situation in the West does not appear to be any better.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Residents in Nanyang have voiced their frustrations over prolonged wait times at hospital A&E departments, with some even having to endure further delays in securing a hospital bed, often relegated to corridors along hospital wards.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This figure pales in comparison to countries like the United States – 2.8 beds; China – 5.2 beds; and Japan – 12.6 beds.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In light of our ageing population, I would like to ask the Minister for Health if he believes that we have insufficient number of hospital beds in Singapore right now.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, is MOH prepared to expedite the construction of additional hospitals beyond those already slated for development?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, many residents in the West, particularly those in Nanyang, encounter difficulties securing appointments at Pioneer Polyclinic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Given the demographic shift towards an ageing population, I would like to inquire whether MOH has plans to build additional polyclinics in Jurong West to alleviate these concerns.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, this success raises concerns about whether we have enough doctors to meet healthcare demands.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many young Singaporeans, including residents from Nanyang, possess a strong desire to pursue careers in medicine.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Unfortunately, the doors to the local medical schools remain largely closed to the majority, despite their excellent results.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is disheartening to note that Singaporean students with perfect GCE "A" level scores of 90 points have been turned away from our medical schools.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Given our ageing population, there is room for an increase in the number of doctors in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to inquire if MOH is prepared to collaborate with the Ministry of Education (MOE) to expand the number of vacancies in the medical schools at NUS, NTU and Duke-NUS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, I also receive feedback that junior doctors in local public hospitals have overwhelming workloads, particularly during their housemanship.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, during a recent cycling trip to Serangoon East Dam, I was dismayed to witness a group of teenagers openly vaping.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Regrettably, similar incidents seem commonplace, as echoed by my residents from their experiences.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: One friend, in particular, recounted reporting a vaping incident to the Police.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Then the Police redirected her to the Health Sciences Authority (HSA).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Despite her complaint, there was no follow-up from HSA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Probably, HSA does not have sufficient resources to follow-through.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Vaping poses a significant problem in schools, with many students obtaining vaping accessories from family members, including their parents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To combat this issue, we must intensify the efforts to raise awareness about the harms of vaping and promote responsible behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Initiatives, such as the "Truth Initiative" campaign by the United States' Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have proven to be effective in reducing vaping prevalence through public education.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While education is crucial, strict enforcement is equally necessary.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We are pleased with the recent Government measures to curb vaping imports and restrict its use in schools and public spaces.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, questions linger regarding the adequacy and effectiveness of the enforcement actions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is concerning that the Chairman and CEO of HSA did not even mention anything about enforcement action against vaping in their messages on the website.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: On the website, the messages are on the front of the website; no mention about anti-vaping measures.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If the Minister is not satisfied, I would question whether relying solely on HSA as the enforcement authority against vaping is sufficient.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Considering the Government's concern that vaping is harmful, I would like to ask the Minister whether the Minister thinks that vaping is more harmful than smoking or it is about the same as smoking.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But if vaping is harmful and we think that we need to enforce with greater strength, I would like to suggest that agencies like the Central Narcotics Bureau and the Police, with their larger enforcement personnel, could assist in the anti-vaping efforts.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, I want to declare my interest as an ophthalmologist in a private group practice.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The issue of healthcare costs and productivity is one that weighs heavily on the minds of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While we strive for accessibility, quality of care for all, rising costs and long waiting times paint a concerning picture for all of us.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Long wait times for appointments and procedures frustrate patients and strain the healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Government has taken steps to address these concerns and increased hospital bed capacity and medical personnel recruitment are commendable efforts.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But all these belated responses are after years of groundswell feedback and growing pressure.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The prompt question now is: why now, when the bed capacity issue has been a concern for years, even before COVID-19?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This reactive approach highlights a need for a more proactive as well as an anticipatory strategy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is being done now to move towards a more forward-looking approach in healthcare administration?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What are the key drivers to cost escalation in healthcare delivery?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are these primarily driven by medical technology advancements, rising drug prices, inflation or other factors or all of the above?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are there specific areas, such as medications, technology as well as administrative costs, that drive cost increases?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This raises serious concerns about accessibility and affordability of essential medication within our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We need to understand the root cause of this behaviour and explore solutions that prioritise both public health as well as affordability.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What specific measures are being taken to slow down cost increases?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We need concrete actions, be it exploring alternative treatment options, revisiting procurement strategies or leveraging on technology for cost optimisation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are there plans to leverage on more bulk purchasing, negotiate for better pricing with pharmaceutical companies or explore alternative treatment options completely?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can MOH explore how we can further expand the capacity of day surgeries to moderate our medical cost increases and reduce inpatient hospitalisation?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Ministry also elaborate on the utilisation of smart solutions and artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare delivery?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can these technologies be used to optimise resource allocation, streamline administrative processes or personalise healthcare for individual patients, leading to cost savings as well as improved outcomes?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Smart medical monitoring devices or wearables can be used to substitute and reduce the reliance on our nurses for patient monitoring in the hospitals and, in same cases, outpatient settings as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is often driven by a lack of knowledge about recognising and managing their health conditions.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While long-term education efforts are crucial, we also need immediate solutions to address the current strain.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Leveraging smart solutions and AI-powered triage systems can be a game-changer.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Patients can rely on virtual consultations to connect with healthcare professionals remotely for initial assessments, potentially avoiding unnecessary A&E visits.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: AI-powered tools with symptom checkers and decision-support tools can also guide patients towards appropriate care options based on their symptoms, directing them to clinics, pharmacies or telemedicine consultations instead of the A&E.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While I acknowledge the Government's efforts to address healthcare challenges, there remains a need for a more proactive, data-driven and cost-conscious approach.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By embracing innovation, empowering patients and leveraging technologies, we can navigate the crossroads of healthcare costs as well as productivity, ensuring accessible, affordable and quality healthcare for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, today, I raise a matter of urgent concern: the need for financial assistance for those living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: SMA is a rare and debilitating genetic disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I got to know Ms Sherry Toh, a 25-year-old socio-political and gaming journalist who lives with SMA type 2.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: SMA is a progressive disease that affects the nervous system and muscles, resulting in severe physical disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the challenges posed by SMA, Sherry is an incredibly resilient person, determined to live her life to the fullest.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Roche, which markets the drug, donated a three-month supply to Sherry last year.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This intervention led to noticeable improvements in her energy levels, swallowing abilities and overall well-being.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It gave Sherry a newfound taste of freedom and independence, enabling her to live her life more fully.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Risdiplam needs to be consumed daily and consistently for its effects to last.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is far beyond the reach of an average Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As soon as the third day without medication, Sherry felt a notable deterioration.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It took her longer to swallow water compared to when she had been on Risdiplam for two months.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While there is hope that SMA treatments may be included in the Rare Disease Fund in the future, I raised this topic in my Parliamentary Question last year, patients like Sherry cannot afford to wait any longer.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Crowdfunding is not a suitable nor sustainable alternative.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Sherry has extended her crowdfunding campaign many times now.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sherry is only trying to buy time, time to witness policy change, time to hope for a brighter tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One in four Singaporeans is expected to develop cancer in their lifetimes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A study last September commissioned by DBS Bank and conducted by Black Box Research surveyed approximately 1,200 participants on their financial readiness to tackle cancer costs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Three key findings emerged: first, that responders perceived difficulty coping with the cost of cancer care; second, that cost concerns may significantly impact decisions about treatment; and third, part of the solution lay in improving financial literacy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Among those surveyed on why they did not purchase additional coverage, some cited unaffordable premiums and a lack of understanding about policy benefits.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One in three participants expressed concerns about the exorbitant cost of cancer care.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: An earlier study by National University Cancer Institute and Research for Impact showed that patients of lower socioeconomic status were at higher risk of financial toxicity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Financial toxicity means that patients are likely to experience significant financial distress due to the cost of care, which usually coincides with a period of lost income.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This not only affects their quality of life and mental well-being, but also that of their family members.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Empowering people early with financial knowledge on private insurance options would instill confidence to prepare for the unexpected catastrophic medical expenditure and allow patients to focus on treatment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is also important to ensure that the national coverage for cancer under MediShield Life remains meaningful.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How is the Ministry working with the relevant stakeholders to raise awareness of cancer treatment costs and to mitigate financial toxicity?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, last July, the Government amended the law to allow women between 21 and 37 years old to undergo elective egg freezing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) supports this as it provides women with the option to preserve fertility and their chances of having children later in life.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is necessary as young Singaporeans are getting married later and our TFR has fallen to 0.97 in 2023.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we can do more to support women who are thinking of or currently undergoing egg freezing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are only certain subsidies that couples can avail of when undergoing in vitro fertilisation (IVF) treatment, if and when they choose to use the frozen eggs in the future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if young women cannot afford to freeze their eggs at the optimal age, there will be no frozen eggs for couples to use later.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conditions on subsidies can be imposed to prevent abuse and ensure that unutilised frozen eggs can be donated to other couples or used for other purposes like research or education.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Countries like South Korea, Japan, Australia and France already subsidise elective egg freezing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can also encourage businesses to subsidise or cover the costs of such procedures and other fertility treatments as part of a package of fertility benefits for their employees.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is already common in the US, where many large employers routinely provide generous coverage for fertility treatments such as egg freezing and IVF as part of their employee benefits.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should encourage this to become the norm in a Singapore made for families.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Young women should be given fertility information through healthcare providers and institutes of higher learning.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would include information about contraception, pregnancy and fertility treatments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Space must be created for young women to have informed conversations about fertility and maternal health issues, so that they can be empowered to make decisions that are best for themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many couples tell me of the long waits at public hospitals for IVF procedures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Co-funding support from the Government is important to allow couples to access IVF which is extremely expensive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there is no support when couples go to private clinics for IVF.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Channeling some couples to private clinics will help ease the load on our public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no fiscal loss to the Government.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For couples who have failed twice at public hospitals, this allows them to try a different approach to increase the chances of success.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are doing so much to get Singaporeans to have children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Couples undergoing IVF are a group that is trying so hard to have children and we are not doing enough to help them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Prime Minister Lee talked about how couples who want kids put off starting families, not realising how quickly it gets harder with each passing year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Couples are starting their families late and a study showed that Singaporean couples try for 3.4 years to conceive before seeking help if they are unable to conceive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Early fertility screening helps people catch problems early and avoid even more costly fertility treatments later when they are older and when it is harder to conceive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not only does it save costs, but it also saves couples from the heartache and stress of multiple rounds of unsuccessful IVF if needed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can view this also as cost savings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, spending more on fertility testing at an early stage might reduce future spending on subsidies for repeated IVF cycles as the success rates of IVF decreases with age.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have raised this previously and I am asking again that the Government provide more subsidies for fertility screening and create a separate MediSave category for fertility screening.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All of us are grateful for the life-saving work of our nurses and healthcare workers during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They put themselves on the frontline to save lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They were stretched during COVID-19, and we all hoped that things will get better for them post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my Budget speech last year, I spoke up for more rest time for nurses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The ANGEL scheme announced by MOH is a positive move.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But in addition to financial incentives, nurses hope we can do more to ensure they have sufficient rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For already exhausted nurses, they dread the PM-AM-PM-AM shift, or PAPA shift.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that nurses work two consecutive sets of afternoon shifts followed by morning shifts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that Khoo Teck Puat Hospital has looked into PAPA shifts and has made positive changes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MOH ensure that all hospitals do away with this PAPA shift and that we look into ensuring nurses have a minimum amount of rest between shifts, similar to what we do for flight attendants?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They should also receive additional MediSave top-ups and more subsidies for intermediate and long-term care.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All this will help persons with disabilities or special needs and their families to defray their medical expenses, which are likely to be larger over their lifetimes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to suggest that MOH track the number of individuals under CHAS who are persons with disabilities or special needs, so as to better understand the healthcare expenses and needs of this group of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has one of the world's toughest anti-smoking laws.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, continuing to raise tobacco taxes and extending public smoking bans may start seeing diminishing returns.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Stricter rules in public places have ironically driven smokers to light up at home or create informal smoking corners, harming their children's health and sparking neighbour complaints about second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: New Zealand initially implemented a cohort smoking ban, but the new Conservative Government revoked it to fund tax cuts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong stated in January 2024 that public health and not potential tobacco tax revenue loss were factors in banning e-cigarettes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I trust this principle will also apply to any Government decision on cohort smoking ban.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A generational smoking ban is specifically designed to safeguard the future without imposing restrictions on current smokers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Hospital bills and insurance premiums continue to rise.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The shift to preventive care under Healthier SG will be a critical lever to bending the cost curve in the long term.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we must also drive cost reduction in the here and now.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have residents who come to us complaining that the cost of medical treatment is higher in Singapore than in the region, but even other wealth developed nations like Japan, that the cost of unsubsidised consultations are sometimes more expensive in our polyclinics that at private GPs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yes, there is a rise in chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yes, we are disadvantaged as a small and rich nation when it comes to drug pricing, but what are the other material drivers of rising health costs that could be controlled?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Healthcare economics is a complex field, rife with principal-agent problems, moral hazards, human emotions and behaviours, and the Government has worked hard to address these challenges over time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But there are proven levers to reduce costs – value-based heathcare, digital technology, strategic procurement – but for their impact to be sustained, changes to ways of working, processes, people and incentives all have to be aligned; otherwise, the costs come back or just move somewhere else.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can we get individuals to make decisions for the good of their loved ones and society as a whole?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What more is being done to keep healthcare costs under control?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: During the Healthier SG White Paper debate, I spoke about value-based healthcare, which is a transformative model of healthcare that focused on delivering better health outcomes with the same or lower costs by optimising available resources, citing several international best practices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung had assured the House then that our hospitals have always been implementing value-based healthcare, have also been through many such initiatives, such as community measures to help resuscitate out of hospital cardiac arrests.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am heartened that we have seen many successful value based healthcare pilots in our healthcare system that demonstrate the potential.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: However, to fully realise this potential, we must scale up these pilots and integrate them across our healthcare system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This requires a concerted effort involving multiple stakeholders across the health care continuum.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must invest in technology, infrastructure, data, workforce training and culture to support this transition and ensure incentives are tied to outcomes, as well as address disparities in access to care and social determinants of health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By embracing value-based care models and scaling up successful pilots, we can improve patient outcomes, enhance health care quality and bend the cost curve.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Digital technology and AI are rapidly transforming the healthcare landscape around the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Digitisation and automation of healthcare systems, has the potential to both improve health outcomes and reduce costs in every area of the industry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The rapid development in GenAI has exciting promises in healthcare, with many emerging AI use cases from aspects as diverse as healthcare R&D, consumer billing and other efficiency, productivity and cost improvements.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The roll-out of the National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) and the Next Gen Electronic Medical Record (EMR) alongside Healthier SG, adds vast array of new sources of data, AI and GenAI, offering exciting opportunities to improve preventive care and empower patients to manage their own healthcare.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Alternative health care models are also gaining momentum.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Telehealth is advancing further, moving from consultations to remote diagnostics, including using AI to analyse symptoms and enable at home lab tests.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Wearables and at home smart medical devices are also being rolled out.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Virtual hospital wards will facilitate the remote continuous monitoring of patients, helping to reduce demands on hospital beds and manpower as well as reduce the need for hospital trips.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What has been the impact thus far, and how do we ensure that these efforts drive sustainable value creation and outcomes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While the focus on healthcare costs discussions often centres around the costs of medical treatments and procedures, the ancillary costs associated with healthcare are often overlooked.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These include medication, transportation and caregiving expenses, and they can add up very quickly to become a significant financial burden.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, transportation costs can be particularly significant for patients with mobility needs, patients who need access to health services frequently, patients with elderly caregivers, and caregivers who do not stay in the same household.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For many families, the Home Caregiver Grant barely begins to cover their caregiving costs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And while the chronic tier of Healthier SG is welcome, patients still face high costs of medications and consumables.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is imperative that we recognise and address these ancillary costs to ensure equitable access to healthcare for all.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This requires a comprehensive approach that encompasses various facets of healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Has the Minister studied the ancillary cost burden for patients under different scenarios?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What support can the Government provide to alleviate this burden for more families?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: On a recent house visit, I met Mdm G who is her 90s.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She has multiple medical conditions and is bedridden.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They sought my help to apply for medical escort services as they struggle to lift her into a wheelchair for her frequent trips to the hospital.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: On the same visit, I met Mdm M who takes care of her special-needs grandson.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In her 70s, Mdm M has her own health problems and she was very worried about who would take care of her grandson when she is gone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As our population ages, many caregivers are ageing or already elderly themselves, grappling with their own age-related health issues, financial constraints and social isolation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The toll of caregiving can be immense physically, emotionally and financially.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the challenges are particularly significant when the caregivers themselves are ageing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What can we learn from other aged societies?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What other scalable solutions are there to address this issue?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, as a member of the People's Action Party's (PAP's) Senior Group, I am delighted to hear about the added emphasis by MOH to strengthen home-care services and options for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Most seniors, even when they get frail, prefer to age-in-place in the comfort of their homes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some seniors are fortunate to have their loved ones who can serve as caregivers or can afford to hire full-time caregivers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This could mean a different option for our seniors, especially if the companies bring on board well-trained caregivers who can serve multiple seniors, say, living in the same HDB precinct.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The next question is whether MOH can share more details broadly about the single-point of contact and how this effort is complementary to the personal health plan which is part of Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to bring up an area of work called Caregiver Equipping and seek a review on whether MOH or the Ministry of Social Family Development (MSF) should be the lead agency in charge of this.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: While MOH rightly takes care of healthcare, the support and enabling of caregivers should be a community effort with the national strategy of ageing-in-place and, hence, should fall within MSF's purview.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Given the rapidly ageing population, more Singaporeans are finding themselves juggling careers and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Support for them should be made widely available in their neighbourhoods and not be relegated to healthcare settings or experts, which is costly and unsustainable.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In Khatib, we launched the Caregiver Resource Centre last year to bring capacity-building and a network of peer support to caregivers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such services should be ramped up quickly so that every caregiver or prospective caregiver can be prepared and equipped to go on this journey whenever it happens.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents shared with me that they were suddenly thrown into a caregiving situation when their aged parents fall ill or have a fall.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This was also my experience when my mom was diagnosed with cancer.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Just like how the Community Emergency and Engagement Committees (C2Es) is a joint effort between the People's Association and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), now ubiquitous in many neighbourhoods, preparing citizens with first-aid and first-responder skills, a similar platform can be set up between MSF and AIC to prepare Singaporeans for caregiving.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The natural place to locate such premises is next to polyclinics and hospitals, and I urge MOH to work closely and in consultation with MSF, which oversees social service agencies to work closely together in such programmes.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Wan Rizal, take your three cuts together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, in our commitment to foster a healthier Singapore, we confront a persistent challenge that has evolved over the years, combating smoking and its modern counterpart, vaping.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In recent years, the landscape of smoking has shifted dramatically with the emergence of vaping which is often mistakenly perceived as a less harmful alternative to traditional cigarettes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This misconception poses a challenge in our fight against smoking.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We need innovative approaches and robust measures to combat the rise of vaping among Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This evolving challenge leads us to a series of pertinent questions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will there be a review of the legislative penalties related to e-vaporisers?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, would MOH consider intensifying public education campaigns to dispel myths around vaping?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: MOH recognises the complexity of this challenge, understanding that it requires a multifaceted approach that addresses the issues at large and pays close attention to the cultural nuances and specific needs of a diverse population.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Smoking, as we are all aware, is a leading cause of preventable diseases and premature deaths worldwide.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In Singapore, our commitment to creating a healthier nation means taking decisive action to curb this habit and mitigate its impact on society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, would MOH consider forging strong partnerships with community leaders and organisations within these communities?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that through this collaboration, we can create culturally resonant messaging that addresses mental health stigmas and increases community buy-in to promote healthier lifestyles with sensitivity and effectiveness.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, in the recent Mental Health Motion, the Health Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) brought forth the need for a comprehensive, accessible and compassionate mental health ecosystem, a cornerstone of a resilient and healthier Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our journey towards improving mental healthcare is not just about enhancing services.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about changing perceptions, breaking down stigma and fostering a support system that supports mental well-being at every level.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: MOH has undertaken various initiatives to expand the availability and quality of mental health services.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Furthermore, the Government recognises that mental health is a priority and integral to overall health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, would MOH consider working closely with religious organisations by providing them with the training and support for their staff as we expand into a more community-based approach?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Training staff as Tier 1 care providers to recognise common mental health issues not only aids in intervention but also supports our idea of long-term care and rehabilitation within the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This could alleviate the manpower shortage and make mental healthcare a more flexible and accessible approach.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, it is vital to ensure quality control and efficacy of such platforms, backed by robust research.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We know that the journey is long and we must take it as a marathon, not just a sprint.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, let us move towards a future where mental health is prioritised, supported and integrated into every aspect of our community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must ensure that everyone has the access to the support they need to lead a mentally healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, providing necessary mental health and wellness services and support cuts across many Ministries.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The several Ministries include MOH, MSF, MOE, the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), MOM and MHA.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Seamless continuum of care is essential to delivering the best care to persons with mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Also key will be the continual efforts to reduce stigma and early diagnosis and intervention.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to keep strengthening support networks for recovery in the community.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This Parliament recently called for a whole-of-nation approach to addressing the current and future mental health challenges in our nation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Chairman, I thank Members for their questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I will start on how we can build a Singapore where our families and seniors can flourish.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Strong families are the building blocks for an ecosystem of care within our communities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They help to ensure the health of their children and are pivotal to supporting our seniors to age well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ageing well starts from home and families should always be the first bastion of care.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Studies show that most seniors prefer to age in the community, close to their families and friends.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Likewise, many families have a desire to care for their loved ones at home.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Age Well SG is led by MOH, the Ministry of National Development (MND), the Ministry of Transport (MOT), with other partner agencies like the People's Association (PA), the Ministry of Social and family Development (MSF) and other volunteer organisations, to enable seniors to lead vibrant and fulfilling lives in the community with their families.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The whole village will work together to realise the Age Well SG plans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First, we will invest in Active Ageing Centres (AACs), which will be a key enabler for seniors to Age Well within the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ultimately, we want seniors to be engaged and connected with their friends and families, which is key to keeping healthy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We would like to make it easier for seniors and families to access available care services and resources in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The AACs are expanding the quality and range of their programmes and adapting their offerings to suit the preferences of seniors living in the vicinity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To make it easier for seniors to join in, most AACs also extend these programmes at community spaces, like PA's Residents' Network.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am told that seniors can participate in classes and activities, and there are also programmes which have been proven to help seniors to age well physically and cognitively.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The National Silver Academy (NSA) offers a diverse range of courses at about 60 AACs, ranging from topics like health and wellness, financial literacy, to information technology and science.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There are also courses for seniors to pick up practical skills, like taking professional photos or floral arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Most of these courses held at the AACs are affordable and around three-quarters of them are eligible for SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about our plans for the roll-out of AACs, our outreach efforts, especially for those who might be socially isolated and how our initiatives can help to foster inter-generational bonding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are scaling up our network of AACs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: AACs serve all seniors regardless of housing type.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, if you have seniors among your loved ones, especially those living on their own, please encourage them to join a nearby AAC.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They help to connect the seniors to community events or activities organised by AACs, such as communal dining.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As such, in addition to participating in activities at the AACs, we also hope for our seniors to join in our efforts in reaching out to other seniors in the community, together with their family and friends.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For about eight years now, Mdm Siah has been actively reaching out to fellow seniors in the community through home visits and telephone engagements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Her spirit has caught on and now her daughter, granddaughter and son-in-law, have also joined in.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are happy that Mdm Siah is finding such meaning in her senior years and their volunteering has fostered and strengthened inter-generational bonds across the family.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ultimately, we want our communities to be places where seniors gather with friends, keep active and stay healthy, starting with AACs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Thirdly, we will enable seniors to be active and move around their neighbourhoods with ease.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MND and the Ministry of Transport (MOT) will be making our flats, neighbourhoods and streets more senior-friendly through EASE 2.0, the upgrading of selected older precincts and MOT's Friendly Streets initiative.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am sure Members have seen how Silver Zones and the lifts at Pedestrian Overhead Bridges bring much joy to our seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will also make enhancements to the home environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Mr Yip Hon Weng would be happy to note that we will also introduce in-flat fall detectors to provide a peace of mind for families with seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: While we want seniors to be able to age in the community, with their families and friends, we recognise that families caring for seniors with care needs may face additional stresses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, we will do more to support these families in caring for their loved ones.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have increased access to home medical care and improved affordability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Today, the Government provides up to 80% means-tested subsidies to patients for home care services such as Home Medical, Home Nursing and Home Therapy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Ms Mariam Jaafar asked about allaying costs beyond medical expenses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MOH's primary focus is to ensure healthcare services are affordable for all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
