text: Our mainstream financing Subsidies, MediShield Life, MediSave, MediFund (S+3Ms) framework, is thus focused on covering acute care, primary care, as well as long-term care services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Nevertheless, we recognise that there are ancillary costs associated with caregiving and that health and social care are closely related.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Hence, MOH has targeted grant schemes to better support families to defray other caregiving expenses, especially for the lower-income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This includes the Medical Escort and Transport (MET) services to help frail seniors attend medical appointments or travel to Senior Care Centres, the Home Caregiving Grant and Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We try to help, but there is a limit to how much we can cover.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Expanding scope of our financing will further push up national healthcare expenditure and ultimately result in a greater burden on people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To better support families and caregivers within the community, we will improve existing services and pilot new care models, as Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Yip Hong Weng and Mr Henry Kwek have suggested.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are studying more options for home care, via an ongoing pilot.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Under "HPC+", seniors are assisted in their daily activities, and this also includes housekeeping services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We thank Mr Henry Kwek for his query on the stay-in shared caregiving sandbox which was launched to mitigate the impact of shrinking family sizes on family caregiving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Under this sandbox, a shared caregiver assists a group of seniors living in public or private estates with their activities of daily living.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This sandbox will be in place for at least a year until the first quarter of 2025.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MOH will review its outcomes and take Mr Henry Kwek's feedback into consideration when determining next steps, which we will announce when finalised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MOH will also introduce standardised care assessments and progressively appoint bundled-services providers, so that seniors can enjoy more seamless care delivery.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This reduces the need for multiple assessments and unnecessary referrals by different care providers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In the interim, the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) works closely with the seniors and their caregivers to make alternative interim care arrangements as needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These efforts will go some way to support families and caregivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We want to make it easier for them to manage the cognitive and physical load of providing care for their loved ones at home.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This includes senior caregivers who may be caring for senior family members.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In addition, we will provide caregivers with resources so that they can be supported in caring for their loved ones.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With these schemes, caregivers can receive more affordable and accessible caregiver training to help them care for their loved ones in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Today, caregivers can access the AIC hotline and online resources available on AIC's website, as well as a Care Services Recommender on the Support-Go-Where portal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will also progressively level up all AACs as community touchpoints to provide information and referral services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, families and caregivers can visit an AAC to discuss how they can obtain the appropriate care for their seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There are also nine AIC links located in public hospitals to provide caregivers who are planning for the discharge of their loved ones from the hospital.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: AIC also runs CREST and COMIT teams that provides support for seniors and caregivers with mental health needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For socio-emotional support, caregivers can also tap on the Caregiver Support Networks (CSNs) and WIN Caregivers Network by PA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Chairman, we have an ambitious vision to be a society where we age well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are rolling out plans in the community that enable seniors to live active lives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are supporting families in caring for their loved ones.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But, ultimately, it is about the heart ware, each of us looking out for one another, helping our seniors lead vibrant and fulfilling lives in the community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Even as we are investing in more support for our seniors, we are also enhancing support for our young families to have healthy and happy lives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In 2021, we set up the task force on Child and Maternal Health and Well-being, or CAMH in short.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Comprising an interdisciplinary team of policy-makers and practitioners from across the health, social and education domains, the task force came together to explore how children and their families can attain good health and well-being.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They engaged parents and caregivers, brainstormed with partners and developed sound recommendations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A detailed report will be shared later this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One of these recommendations is to enhance support for couples from pre-conception and pregnancy, through to parenthood.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Many parents-to-be recognise that antenatal care is important as they prepare for the birth of their child.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, not all parents have access to resources and support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Those who attend these classes will have convenient access to subsidised antenatal support close to their homes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Couples can look forward to learning about nutrition and exercises during pregnancy and after delivery and be equipped to care for their newborn.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The classes will be conducted via a hybrid model, incorporating online lectures and videos, so that parents can easily access these useful resources virtually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is important that we support and celebrate active fathering too.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In collaboration with the Families for Life Council and Centre for Fathering, we are strengthening the participation of fathers in parents' support groups in schools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will provide more avenues for fathers to share and learn valuable parenting insights and tips.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will continue to support fathers who may require more support in their parenthood journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At the Committee of Supply (COS) debate last year, I shared how the National University Hospital (NUH) expanded the Women's Emotional Health Service Plus (WEHS+) pilot, extending mental health support services to fathers in need.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This support is important at the antenatal and postnatal stages as they take on the new role of a father.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This pilot has also since extended support for mothers up to six years postnatal, up from the previous one year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We want couples to feel supported and assured during their parenthood journey, even and especially when they meet challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As Ms S experienced postnatal depression and anxiety, the team followed up with regular check-ins and emotional support to ensure she was coping well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The team also ensured that her husband received timely assistance and treatment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Both are faring better now and the good news is that Ms S is expecting another baby.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am glad that this programme has given them the confidence and reassurance that they are well-supported in their journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over time, Ms S and her husband will be able to transit to Family Nexus, which supports families with children aged zero to six, enabling them to access cross-domain services at a one-stop community touchpoint near their homes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Last year, I announced the launch of the Family Nexus pilot at Our Tampines Hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am delighted to update that the Family Nexus pilot has been rolled out to three more sites in Singapore, at Choa Chu Kang, Punggol and Sembawang polyclinics, to extend support to more families.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Helping our children pick up good habits for good health during their formative years paves the way for better long-term health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, we want to empower parents with more resources and information to nurture healthy habits in their children.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This, too, is one of the task force's recommendations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: During our engagements, many parents shared that they were on the lookout for accessible and reliable information to support them in nurturing their children.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We shared about Parent Hub in 2022, a one-stop resource portal to provide timely information on pregnancy and parenting to families.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Since its launch, Parent Hub has garnered over three million views, with over 100,000 page views monthly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will continue to expand on these resources, such as by making new interactive evidence-based resources on nurturing healthy eating in childhood and other relevant topics available on the portal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These guidelines support those involved in the care of children aged zero to two in nurturing healthy eating habits, providing goals and milestones in the transition from infant feeding to eating as a young child.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I urge parents, caregivers and healthcare professionals to refer to these guidelines to promote a positive environment for the adoption of healthier eating habits in our young children, which would be beneficial to them in years to come.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will make resources available beyond the early years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Students will be able to access online interactive resources through MOE's Student Learning Space this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These resources will help students learn more about healthier eating habits and ways to have a balanced meal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These efforts are aligned with the GUSTO research study which shows that children's eating behaviours, such as portion size, food choice and nutrition, are key risk factors for childhood obesity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Together, we can build a society where every family is empowered to grow and age well and enjoy a life of health and well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will devote a large part of my speech to address two pressing issues for healthcare: one is the hospital capacity crunch; the other is healthcare cost.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, I will talk about the major transformation that we are bringing about in our healthcare system which will further address these two concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Ang Wei Neng and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim raised the issue of capacity and waiting times at polyclinics and hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Post-COVID-19, indeed, this is the experience of many countries around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Waiting times have gone up all around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is happening against the backdrop of a rapidly ageing population, which compounds the problem and makes it a long-term challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Singh suggested that we provide dynamic waiting times of emergency departments (EDs) across hospitals publicly, in real time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is possible, but we have been reluctant to do so, I think for a good reason.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ambulances today already have a process in place to ferry patients needing urgent care to the nearest appropriate hospital for priority treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, at the EDs, 40% of cases are not life-threatening or urgent, but they ended up there anyway.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, our worry is that giving dynamic information may perversely drive more non-urgent cases to hospitals and worsen the overall situation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I know it is very uncomfortable, very unsettling for a patient who is quite unwell to have to wait many hours for a bed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But please be assured that hospitals will triage patients quickly upon arrival and start treatment for urgent cases, even if the patient is waiting for a bed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng raised the issue of Changi General Hospital which was also reported in a Straits Times article.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the queue will build up quite fast.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But actually, that is not the limiting factor.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What we need to watch out for are Intensive Care Unit (ICU) occupancy, resuscitation occupancy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If those are full, we divert the ambulances.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the surface, it looks bad; but actually, operationally, it is not a huge problem to overcome.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim suggested using more Urgent Care Centres (UCCs).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have also been using the General Practitioner (GP) First scheme, especially around Changi area, and that is also useful, and we will continue to deploy all possible methods to alleviate patient loads at the EDs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They make up the over 11,000 public hospital beds that we have today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we should see new capacity coming on stream every year, from now to 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Starting this year, and next, in 2024 and 2025, Woodlands Health will commission up to 700 beds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2026, Sengkang General Hospital and Outram Community Hospital are expected to expand by about 350 beds by converting non-clinical areas into hospital wards.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then in 2027, the Elective Care Centre at Singapore General Hospital (SGH) is expected to open; that has 300 beds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2028 and 2029, the redeveloped Alexandra Hospital is expected to open progressively.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then in 2029 and 2030, the new Eastern General Hospital Campus is expected to open progressively.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then we move into the early 2030s, that is when we hope to see the completion of a new regional public hospital that we have started work on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have just completed one in the North, Woodlands Health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are building another one in the East.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are expanding SGH in the central region.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will best complement current hospitals in the West.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The new hospital in Tengah will be run by the National University Health System cluster.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng is nodding his head.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Notwithstanding this plan to expand capacity, we should not be trapped in the mindset of "building hospitals" when thinking about capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is potential to better anchor care outside of hospitals, in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not all patients require high acuity care and constant monitoring in a hospital throughout their treatment course.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many need convalescent care and rehabilitation, with the assurance that medical help is readily available nearby.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why we have built more community hospitals for sub-acute and rehabilitation patients, and Transitional Care Facilities for patients who are waiting for longer-term care arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With our efforts, the number of long-staying patients have come down and these are patients defined as medically stable for discharge but they have been staying in the hospitals while waiting for longer-term care and they have been staying for longer than 21 days.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is what we refer to as long-staying patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two years ago, it was about 300 such patients at any one time in our hospital system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, it is under 200 patients at any one time and there is still room for improvement.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To facilitate appropriate transfers from acute hospitals to community settings, we will also be making a few policy changes, as follows.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Acute hospitals have experienced friction in transferring suitable patients to community hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, certain diagnostic services, such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and certain more expensive drugs, are not subsidised in community hospitals today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is based on the consideration that these are recovering patients and they may not need these interventions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Unfortunately, this means operational delays in transferring patients to community hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are patients who are medically ready to be transferred, but they are just waiting for a follow-up scan.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They should be transferred without delay and do the scan at the community hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Others worry that after transfer, what if, unexpectedly, I need a scan for some reason.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, they insist on staying in the acute hospital, just in case.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With this enhancement, most community hospital patients will see smaller hospital bills.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second change is to make Mobile Inpatient Care at Home (MIC@Home) a mainstream service.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a pilot project where we set up virtual hospital beds at the homes of patients, and have doctors and nurses visit them, as if they are in the hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Pritam Singh, Ms Ng Ling Ling and Ms Mariam Jaafar have asked or talked about such a scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the end of last year, more than 2,000 patients have benefited from the scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This translates to around 9,000 hospital bed days saved.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All our hospitals intend to price MIC@Home similar to, or lower than, a normal hospital ward.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Patients will be supported by subsidies, MediShield Life and MediSave, no different from a physical inpatient stay.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In response to Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's suggestion, I do not think we therefore need to give an incentive for transition to home care now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last year, we extended subsidies and allowed the use of MediSave for the use of telehealth, for chronic care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By the second half of this year, we will also expand MediSave coverage to telehealth consults for preventive care services, such as follow-up reviews after regular health screening.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With this change, telehealth is treated almost the same way as physical consultations in terms of financial support.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The only difference is telehealth for common illnesses, that is, when patients experience symptoms, like cough, cold and fever.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Patients still cannot use MediSave for such consults for common illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are holding this back as many people have been using such teleconsults as an easy way to get medical certificates (MCs).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, there will need to be greater discipline in issuing MCs before we consider this final move.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another key aspect to expanding capacity is to enhance manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Dr Tan Wu Meng asked if we need to produce more doctors to meet demand.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Yes, we have been and will continue to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, intakes into our local medical schools have increased by about 30% over the past 10 years, to about 500 now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you consider each cohort, it is now slightly over 30,000.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: About half of them, 15,000 or so, 15,000 to 17,000 go to university; and out of that group, 500 are training to be doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Still, more are training to be Allied Health Professionals and nurses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we are taking quite a lot of talent.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are also offering awards and grants to actively attract Singaporeans who graduated from overseas medical schools back into the local public healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Where does Singapore stand, in terms of our doctor to population ratio?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ours, in terms of practising doctors, is about 2.6.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us put that number into some perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Compared to developing countries, we are ahead, we are higher.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Compared to developed economies in Asia, we are similar.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Korea, Hong Kong and Taiwan are all around 2.6.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Japan is also 2.6 and despite having actually aged much earlier than us, with about 30% of their population 65 and older.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, if you compare to developed Anglo-Saxon countries – the United Kingdom (UK), United States (US), Canada – we are just slightly behind.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is really when we compare to European countries – continental European countries, Australia – that we are a notch behind.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It could be a legacy of the welfare state.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It could be the fact that European countries do not really have a tradition of planning for manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can explore if further increases are needed, but we have to recognise that talent is in short supply across all sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And healthcare, we should attract our fair share, but not disproportionate share of talent.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Beyond this fair share, countries can also end up chasing its own tail.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For one, it is not a simple numbers game.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The right mix of doctors is just as important as the sheer number of doctors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If, somehow, doctors get registered but do not practise, it does not help.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If doctors are practising, but they go into areas like aesthetics, it also does not help very much.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Singapore, graduates from medical schools are already finding it more competitive to get residency positions to be trained as specialists, because there is not much of a shortage in many of these specialist areas.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have also seen in many countries, how supply of doctors creates its own demand.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As more doctors compete for business, there will be a tendency to prescribe more tests, scans, medications and procedures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Patients are not likely to say no because your health is at stake, and especially if healthcare is free or insurance covers all the costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, while Mr Ang Wei Neng provided numbers to show that Singapore's doctor-to-population ratio is lower than some Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries, this did not translate to poorer health outcomes, less accessibility or affordability in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, we know that the US healthcare system is not the most accessible unless you have the right insurance.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The UK's higher doctor-to-population ratio than us, has eight million patients on their waiting lists and is suffering from a chronic capacity crunch.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Germany, also much higher than us in terms of the ratio, is facing a major challenge meeting the healthcare needs of their seniors across their länders or their states.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Conversely, Singapore, we are delivering quite good healthcare outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A commonly accepted broad measure is the expected health span and lifespan of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In short, we have better outcomes with less spending and lower hospital beds and doctors-to-population ratios than many OECD countries, because it is not just a numbers game.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The quality and the mix of doctors, the geographical spread of the country, how the whole system is run, the behaviour of patients – all makes a big difference.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have a lot of room for improvement, but there is no reason to feel bad about ourselves or to envy others.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are, in fact, in a good place as we continue to learn from others and strive for improvements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Chairman, let me now address the next concern, which is rising healthcare costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak, Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms Ng Ling Ling asked, what is driving up healthcare costs?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this section, I will talk about the likely reasons for rising healthcare costs, explain the realities of healthcare financing and then what we are doing to try to moderate costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A major factor for rising healthcare costs is that we are getting older, and as we get older, we are more likely to fall seriously ill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over the last five years, the number of Singaporean seniors increased by almost 20%, from 560,000 to 690,000 now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are on the verge of becoming a super-aged society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are not macro numbers, it directly affects individuals and families.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, when in a family, one member grows older and falls seriously ill, the entire family feels the burden of healthcare costs and also the caregiving burden.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Technological advancement can make a car or a smartphone cheaper and better.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But in healthcare, it is often not the case.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: New treatments may work better, but always cost more.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, advancement in orthopaedic surgeries have made knee replacements much easier to do.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In my constituencies, I met many seniors who have gone through knee replacements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sometimes, they have gone through both and when I meet them – I have gone through one – we end up comparing our battle scars.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the past, people with degenerating blood vessels in their eyes due to old age, they will lose their central vision.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, the condition can be treated and controlled through repeated intravitral injections.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These advancements allow a person who cannot walk, to walk again; allow a person who would have been blind, to see again.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The cost to the patients has also gone up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even for the same treatment, not talking about medical advancement; the same treatment, the cost has gone up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Inflation all around the world has gone up in recent years and that has also affected healthcare costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A key component of healthcare delivery cost is manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Singapore, manpower is more than half of the cost to run the healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We all agree we need to compensate our healthcare workers fairly and competitively.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As healthcare demands have gone up in many countries, the competition for medical manpower is now international and has become more intense.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this pushed up manpower costs and, therefore, healthcare costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when the coverage becomes too generous down to the last dollar, we start to see excessive prescriptions and tests and even unnecessary treatments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the classic buffet syndrome, which has driven up claims.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It has driven up claims and, therefore, it has driven up insurance premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Yet, it is frustrating to see insurance companies continue to offer unsustainable terms – presumably they are competing for market share.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, how do we address rising healthcare costs?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to first recognise two truisms in healthcare financing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first truism is that, ultimately, the people always pay.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When my wife and I moved to Switzerland for a year for me to do my Master's programme, that was in 1999, we had to make a social security payment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I cannot remember the name, but it was not cheap.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A few thousand Swiss francs for the both of us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we do not pay, we could not live in Switzerland.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Each time we visited her, we can just go in and go out.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We paid for it already, through the rather expensive social security fee.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Britain, the National Health Service (NHS) operates by the principle of free healthcare at the point of delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: No UK government has ever touched that principle.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It continues to be free at the point of delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The British have to pay high taxes to finance the NHS, because there is no cost at the point of healthcare delivery, the waiting times at the NHS are very long.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, British patients are also paying with their time and their patience.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are different ways to pay for healthcare: by taxes, by compulsory social security payments, through insurance premiums or personal savings or your personal time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ultimately, the people always pay one way or another.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This leads to the second truism, which is how we pay affects how much we pay.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If a government uses taxes to make healthcare "free" at the point of delivery, then it will likely lead to the buffet syndrome that I just mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There will be over-consumption, wastage and high-cost inflation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If a government leaves the people to buy their own health insurance, people will tend to be very careful, which can moderate healthcare expenditure.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: S+3Ms ensures universality because it provides all Singaporeans access to quality healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is also a targeted system, focusing assistance on those who need it the most.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To illustrate, subsidies of up to 80% are extended to C Class wards in public hospitals, but not A Class wards, not private hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MediShield Life covers a significant part of the remaining bill after subsidy, but we ensure some co-payment by patients, mostly through MediSave, so that there is less of a buffet syndrome.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With these two truisms in mind, what can we do and what are we doing about rising healthcare costs?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, let me start with the S, of S+3Ms.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Subsidies will have a big role to play.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When I first joined the Government in 2015 and entered this House, I was the Acting Minister for Education.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Ministry of Education's (MOE's) budget was the second largest amongst Ministries, at about S$12 billion, and only behind the Ministry of Defence's (MINDEF's).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH's was the distant third, just over S$9 billion.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, nine years later, I am now the Minister for Health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is channeled to fund many aspects of the healthcare system: build new healthcare infrastructure, operate hospitals, polyclinics and nursing homes, procure medicines and equipment, developing new IT systems, hiring doctors, nurses and all our medical personnel.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH's budget is tax-funded and constitutes healthcare subsidies, which have been rising significantly over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, the second M – MediShield Life – will also need to work harder.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MediShield Life, as I mentioned, is a national health insurance scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It covers everyone for life, even those with pre-existing illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is specifically designed for the great majority of subsidised patients who are encountering a major health episode.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It contains a couple of important phrases, which I will explain.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I said it covers great majority of subsidised patients, because most Singaporeans seek subsidised care and the "great majority of them" need financial assistance to foot their healthcare bills.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, for a C Class Ward patient, he will find that after subsidy, MediShield Life claims should substantially pay for the rest of his hospital bill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For a patient that goes to a private hospital, he will find that MediShield Life covers only a modest part of his hospital bill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is how MediShield Life is focused on the subsidised patients, especially those that uses C Class wards.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then "a major health episode", because this upholds the spirit of insurance, which is to protect us against rare occasions when we incur a big hospital bill because we fall seriously ill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With that context, let me report the state of MediShield Life today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was designed such that nine out of 10 subsidised bills are adequately covered.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What remains are relatively small and expected co-payments, which can be paid from MediSave.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, this nine in 10 benchmark is being eroded, because the size of hospital bills is getting even bigger.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Subsidised patients are seeing hospital bills that are unexpectedly large.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And after subsidy and MediShield Life, there is still a substantial out-of-pocket component left.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is when higher healthcare costs really start to bite.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH has, therefore, tasked our MediShield Life Council – which is from various stakeholders led by a private sector person – to comprehensively review the scheme, but we have given the Council some direction.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, enhance MediShield Life to give Singaporeans greater assurance against large bills.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means increasing how much a patient can claim from MediShield Life – this is what we call claim limits – for both surgeries and hospital stays.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We envisage a fairly significant increase in the claim limits.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also need to raise the claim limits for treatments, such as kidney dialysis, to reduce out of pocket expenses for patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Council will also explore extending coverage to more types of outpatient care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of the most costly outpatient treatments are for cancer.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked if we could improve financial literacy for patients to better plan against such a disease.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are resources available online and we will raise the public's awareness to them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I think the issue goes beyond financial literacy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are facing an especially difficult challenge for cancer, as treatment costs were rising uncontrollably.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I am not surprised at the survey results that you cited at all.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, we recently reviewed cancer drug financing and introduced changes that will allow us to negotiate for lower prices for cancer drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The impact is still playing out and we will continue to monitor the situation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, the Council will consider expanding MediShield Life coverage to new groundbreaking treatments, specifically Cell, Tissue and Gene Therapy Products (CTGTPs).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Medical science is advancing rapidly and CTGTPs have the potential to revolutionise healthcare and deliver effective treatment of previously incurable diseases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some describe these as the equivalent of a moonshot for healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Essentially, the treatment involved is, we extract blood from a patient, then with the blood, you teach and equip the cells in the blood to target and kill, say, cancer cells, then you put the cells back into the patient's body to do its work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, while the technology is promising and advancing fast, it is nascent and very expensive.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It could cost anything from a few hundred thousand dollars to a few million dollars, per treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want to start including CTGTPs under MediShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But, we need to put in place safeguards to ensure that financing of CTGTPs is sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For instance, we will need to extend MediShield Life coverage only to treatments that are assessed to be safe, clinically effective and cost effective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In other words, if a treatment costs a few million dollars with a small hope of curing a small group of people, it is not cost effective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a significant step to help all Singaporean patients, regardless of their income levels, have access to cost effective, novel, state-of-the-art therapies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These proposed changes will better protect subsidised patients against major health episodes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MediShield Life premiums, however, will inevitably go up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But, rest assured that we will do the necessary to ensure that, as far as possible, premiums can be paid fully by MediSave.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, we will consider enhancing premium subsidies, or have MediSave top-ups for specific groups.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We may have to use more MediSave for small hospital bills, so that MediShield Life can better focus on big hospital bills, and in that way, we moderate premium increases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: No one will lose MediShield Life coverage due to a genuine inability to afford the premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will share more details when the Council completes its review in the second half of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chair, while we address these immediate concerns, we should not lose sight of the longer-term, strategic direction of healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is, continue to build health and not just treat illnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have crystalised this strategy around Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Dr Syed Harun asked for an update on Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am very glad to say that it has been progressing encouragingly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a good split, because a key thrust of Healthier SG is to empower our GPs to play a greater role in population health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over half of the enrollees have started consulting their chosen doctors to develop a personal Health Plan and they have been rewarded S$20 worth of Healthpoints.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over the past year, the number of participants in exercise sessions organised by the Health Promotion Board (HPB) has increased by 16%, from 133,000 to 154,000.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For sessions organised by PA, participation has gone up 12%, from about 400,000 to 450,000.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For SportSG's sessions, it has increased by 20%, from 117,000 to 140,000.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we see a discernible increase in people becoming active and individuals are also up and about on their own.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling asked if we expect prevalence rate of chronic illnesses to come down due to Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With a strong start to Healthier SG, we certainly hope this will happen.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have recently raised chronic drug subsidies for Healthier SG enrollees seeking care at their Healthier SG GP clinics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the coming year, we plan to implement further improvements to the scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: GPs are guided by Healthier SG Protocols, to ensure that residents enjoy consistent and quality care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are 12 protocols so far, which include screening, vaccination and management of common chronic diseases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will start to roll them out in early 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As announced earlier, we are also starting to work on including aspects of mental health into the protocols.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Currently, your enrolled doctor will co-develop a health plan with you as part of the preventive care consultation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It covers essential action items, such as regular health screening and vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But on the lifestyle, the advice is always quite generic, such as "exercise more", "eat better".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2024, we will start to make the advice more specific.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, it may recommend you do aerobic exercise three times a week.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can then use the Healthy 365 app to identify suitable exercise activities near your home.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Key features in Healthy 365 will be made multilingual.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, we will continue to roll out interventions for our seniors through the Age Well SG programme, which Second Minister Masagos has elaborated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fourth, we will continue to fight against overconsumption of sugar and sodium.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our Nutri-Grade labelling of pre-packaged drinks have been useful in changing consumer behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will regularly and personally inspect the drinks in the Members' Room.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am glad to report they are all graded "A" and "B", and passed the MOH Ministerial inspection.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is one drink, however, "zero sugar salty lychee".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, I texted my staff to say what do we label this for?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I also encountered students who are asking for less sugar in their bubble tea, so that it qualifies for Nutri-Grade "B".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the Minister for Education, I always tell students, do not be so grade conscious.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But in this case, it is good to be grade conscious and go for "A" and "B".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have recently extended Nutri-Grade to freshly made beverages.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I met the two key coffee shop associations recently and sought their support.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Together they represent over half of the coffee shops in Singapore, and they intend to start serving "siu dai" or less sugar beverages by default.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means when you order a kopi in future, they give you "siu dai", even though you do not say it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you want even less sugar, I recommend just drink "kosong".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sodium is the other culprit that can lead to heart diseases and strokes, if over-consumed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is found in salt, soya sauce, belachan and other sauces.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: About 30% of the catering industry are supporting our "Less Salt, More Taste" movement since it was launched late last year. 20% of the food and beverage industry are also doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I recently saw an encouraging programme on Channel 8.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There were two lady hosts, they went on a 21-day challenge to take less salt and less soya sauce.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the end of the 21 days, their blood pressure measurements had moderated somewhat, but more importantly, their taste buds had become much more sensitive to salt.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They could now taste the ingredients better, they never knew when they taste something, there are undertones of garlic, ginger, spices.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They used to just taste soya sauce and belachan, and they prefer to eat less salt now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It took 21 days to change a lifelong habit.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Remember, because we eat every day, the effect of food accumulates through our lifetimes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over our lifetimes, food can be medicine, food can also be poison.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a wise traditional chinese medicine (TCM) physician once told me, if you eat well, there is no need for medicine; if you do not eat well, medicine is of little use.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, Dr Tan Wu Meng urged that healthcare needs to be delivered across time and space, which we agree.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is, in fact, a key aspect of the transformation we are striving for.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whereas sickness often needs to be treated in clinics and hospitals, health almost exclusively has to be built up in communities and in our homes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH has been working on this transformation and we have made a few strategic policy changes over the last couple of years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Patient data needs to flow across care delivering settings, from hospitals to clinics, to senior care and rehabilitation centres.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What remains is a new law, which I hope to table in this House in the later part of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Financial support needs to be settings and premises neutral.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we cannot simply apply this based on first principles, as it is bound to lead to abuse and unintended behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most importantly, we need to be decisive and deliberate in making investments in preventive care and health of our population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We often hear calls for investment in hospital capacity, in our medical manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But what is more important for the long term is capacity expansion in communities and society, in its ability to prevent sickness and build health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are doing so via Healthier SG, and we are starting to see a change.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: More residents are coming forward to exercise, cycle, run or brisk walk.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Food and beverage (F&B) players are switching to lower-sodium salt.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Christine Lock, who sells nasi lemak, she was the first to do so at Bukit Canberra Hawker Centre.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She did so voluntarily, because she had a loved one who suffered a heart attack.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She said, "I want to take care of my customers." Film Director Jack Neo has started a brisk walking group for seniors, started during the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In English, it means walking around for fun.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: His event is every week, and it will attract almost 1,000 participants, young and old, from all over Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If they descend on one of your communities, you will immediately notice.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For them, brisk walking has become a new habit, and they made new friends.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Jack and his team even composed a song about "趴趴走" and incorporated messages of Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, when I joined them two weeks ago, everyone sang the song.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many Members will know her, she was a former Member of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She agreed to let me share her story with you today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She enrolled into Healthier SG late last year, with a GP clinic near her home.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The GP noticed that she had not done a mammogram for three years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That was when Cynthia found out that she might have breast cancer and it was later confirmed through a biopsy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She has since gone through an operation to remove the tumour and no further tumours were discovered in her body.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She wants me to tell everyone – please push for Healthier SG in your communities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You know how persistent Cynthia can be when she calls for action, because it can change lives and it can save lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The UK Legatum Institute ranks healthcare systems in the world in a holistic manner.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a valuable vote of confidence in our system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It encourages us to improve and do better.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is said that there is an unbreakable iron triangle in healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The three aims in healthcare: affordability, quality and accessibility.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are also trade-offs, such that improvement in one area always comes at the expense of the other two areas.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have outlined how, by using MIC@Home and right-siting, we can increase capacity without necessarily building more hospital beds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In other words, improve accessibility, without compromising quality of care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By weaving insurance and co-payment, we reduce out-of-pocket payment for patients, while containing excessive demand for healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And more importantly, by building better health through Healthier SG, we achieve all three aims at the same time and enable people to lead longer, healthier and more meaningful lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthier SG is not a Government programme or a financing scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a movement for Singaporeans, a new way of life, a new compact between people, the community and the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We may not have broken the iron triangle to open a straight and easy line to good health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we have made a good start and carved our own path to achieve greater happiness and probably prosperity, depending on how you look at it, for ourselves, our families and our nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As we age, we become more susceptible to developing serious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As a nation, we have become less healthy in the past decade, with a general rise in the prevalence of chronic diseases, such as hypertension.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Life expectancy in Singapore has improved over the last 10 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Seniors are increasingly living alone, and this trend is expected to continue as our population ages and average household size decreases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For all these reasons and others, the strain on individuals and their families and the impact on our healthcare system will increase significantly in the coming years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to strengthen our healthcare system to meet these challenges by proactively encouraging healthier lifestyles and preventing or delaying the onset of poor health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This involves strengthening healthcare services in the community closer to individuals' everyday environment and leveraging our extensive network of family doctors and community partners as necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: While we continue to invest in building new healthcare infrastructure, upgrading existing ones, we are also expanding our primary and community care services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Studies have shown that individuals with a regular family doctor experience better health outcomes, including fewer hospitalisations and emergency department visits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Beyond managing our acute and chronic illnesses, the primary care team also plays a vital role in preventing the onset of serious illnesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: An ongoing relationship with a regular doctor allows for deeper understanding and familiarity with patients' medical conditions, sensitivities to medications and foods, and their day-to-day lives of the patient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The existing Clementi Polyclinic and Jurong Polyclinic will also be redeveloped by 2030 to increase their capacities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I agree with Dr Tan Wu Meng on the need to ensure adequate accessibility between polyclinics and major transportation nodes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For the redeveloped Clementi Polyclinic, MOH has worked with the Land Transport Authority (LTA) to ensure that sheltered pedestrian access will be provided between the building and Clementi MRT station's nearest exit, save for the junction across Clementi Ave 3, where such shelters will not be practical, because the junction is wide and there are double-decker buses passing through.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As our society ages, we need to ensure that seniors' social and health needs are adequately supported in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Having strong social support networks have been shown to contribute to better health outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is particularly important for seniors who live alone and are at risk of social isolation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: AACs will collaborate with healthcare providers, including family doctors, as well as work with other community providers and Government agencies for active ageing programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addition to physical health, we also need to look after our mental health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: At the Parliament Motion on advancing mental health last month, this House recognised the importance of mental health as a health, social and economic issue, and affirmed the importance of a robust national mental health ecosystem to enhance mental health and well-being.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Keith Chua asked about key areas that the National Mental Health Office (NMHO) will be focusing on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It will oversee the implementation of various plans under the National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy and shape the development of future mental health initiatives, building upon previous efforts such as the National Mental Health Blueprint and the Community Mental Health Masterplan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Under the Office, we will scale up mental health services in the primary and community care settings and strengthen access to community-based care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Specifically, initial plans include building the competencies of professionals and frontline personnel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will include staff in religious organisations to support persons with mental health needs, to address Dr Wan Rizal's question about involving religious organisations in community mental health support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Other plans include promoting early care access through publicising key mental health first-stop touchpoints and ensuring better care coordination among service providers through the development of a practice guide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The Office will also track indicators to monitor the progress and outcomes of these plans, as reflected in the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy Report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: While persons with severe mental health conditions may seek psychiatric care at hospitals, those with mild to moderate mental health symptoms would benefit more from care delivered in the community, as compared to being institutionalised for treatment or being removed from their daily routines and social networks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Dr Syed Harun asked if mental health will be a focus of Healthier SG implementation plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In addition, over 450 GPs have been trained to support persons with mental health needs under the Mental Health General Practitioner Partnership (MHGPP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH will also be developing mental health protocols and incorporating mental health care and support, as part of the scope of practice for GPs in Healthier SG clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will also be strengthening mental health outreach and intervention in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Today, we have 73 Community Outreach Teams (CREST) that detect and help individuals with mental health needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These teams support GPs in the provision of psychosocial interventions for persons with mental health needs in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This also addresses Dr Wan Rizal's question on what is being done to enhance the accessibility and integration of mental health services within the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our primary care teams need to be suitably sized and equipped with the right skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They also need to be adequately supported to provide team-based and integrated care, through Primary Care Networks (PCNs) and consultations with specialists and by leveraging on technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng highlighted the need to ensure GPs in participating Healthier SG GP clinics have the necessary resources and expertise to effectively manage chronic conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling also asked how the Government intends to support the professional development of GPs, especially in areas that they may be increasingly involved in, such as social prescriptions to influence patients' lifestyle choices for better health outcomes and treatment of common mental health conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Dr Syed Harun asked about retention plans for healthcare professionals to support Healthier SG and the shift towards preventive health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOH is working closely with Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to increase local training pipelines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are also committed to the development of family doctors in primary and community care and have placed a stronger emphasis on family medicine training, such as encouraging more doctors to take up postgraduate Family Medicine training like the Graduate Diploma in Family Medicine (GDFM) and the Masters of Medicine in Family Medicine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Postgraduate training in Family Medicine is also strengthened to help family doctors be more equipped to manage a wider range of complex conditions across different age groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Training is delivered through various modalities including video conferencing and webinar platforms, allowing GPs more flexibility as they keep up to date with the latest developments in family medicine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: At the same time, we are increasing the number of nurses, pharmacists and other allied health professionals in the community, and are providing interdisciplinary training to empower them to practise at the highest level of their licences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will also expand the role of community pharmacists and other allied health professionals in primary and community care to improve care delivery in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These are non-medically trained persons who can undertake tasks, such as arranging the initial health screening and coordinating referrals to community programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Healthcare professionals can then focus on clinical care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Primary care teams will be supported with Healthier SG Care Protocols to ensure consistent, quality care for patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These care protocols lay out clear processes, referrals and data flows to guide GPs in managing each health condition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: More care protocols will be developed to cover more chronic diseases in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We recognise that some GPs may have more experience in managing certain chronic conditions than others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Therefore, we will work closely with the College of Family Physicians Singapore (CFPS), AIC and healthcare clusters to roll out training for GPs and their care teams for each care protocol.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will also support GPs in the provision of holistic care for patients with mental health needs by strengthening the links to COMIT for non-pharmacological mental health support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As we mobilise family doctors to co-develop health plans with their patients, which can include adjustments to lifestyles and regular health screening, we expect that the percentage of patients requiring longer clinic consultations to increase.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This has been taken into account when planning for future primary care capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To allow family doctors to focus on optimising clinical care, we have adopted a team-based care approach in polyclinics and private GP clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In polyclinics, patients with chronic conditions are assigned to multidisciplinary care teams comprising family physicians, nurse care managers and care coordinators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In private GP clinics, PCNs anchor and strengthen team-based care for chronic diseases, by pooling resources to organise core ancillary services provided by nurses and care coordinators who work with GPs to jointly manage the patients' conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our clusters will also step up as regional health managers, working with family doctors and other partners to address health and social needs of residents in their region and anchor care in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Family doctors may work with specialists or hospital doctors in the management of patients with more complex needs, for example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Upon discharge, the hospitals would refer patients to the family doctor they are enrolled with, to ensure continuity of care between the hospital space and the primary care space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
